extracted.intended_audience: Attorneys and practitioners who represent trademark applicants before the USPTO; USPTO disciplinary officers and legal compliance officers
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and regulatory requirements governing ethical practice, supervision, signature rules, financial handling, and consequences for USPTO trademark practitioners, including rules on resignation and reinstatement. Focused on discipline/exclusion on consent under USPTO regulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.101 — Competent representation
rubrics_metrics.description: It is professional misconduct if a practitioner fails to provide competent representation to a client.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Competent representation includes the legal knowledge, skill, thoroughness, and preparation reasonably necessary for the representation. Practitioners representing trademark applicants are reasonably expected to be knowledgeable of USPTO regulations and guidance (e.g., electronic signing rules) relevant to their practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.105(b) — Communicate scope of representation and fees
rubrics_metrics.description: It is professional misconduct if a practitioner fails to communicate the scope of the representation and the basis or rate of the fee and expenses for which the client will be responsible before or within a reasonable time after commencing the representation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners must disclose fee structure and scope timely; failing to do so can constitute misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.115(a) — Hold client/third-party property separately
rubrics_metrics.description: It is professional misconduct if a practitioner fails to hold property of clients or third persons that is in a practitioner's possession in connection with a representation separate from the practitioner's own property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Client funds and property must be segregated from practitioner assets; commingling is misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.115(c) — Client trust account deposits and withdrawals
rubrics_metrics.description: It is professional misconduct if a practitioner fails to deposit into a client trust account legal fees and expenses that have been paid in advance, or withdraws from the trust account those fees and expenses before the fees are earned or expenses are incurred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advance payments that are client funds must be held in trust until earned; practitioners must follow proper trust accounting and withdrawal rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.303(a)(1) — False statements to the USPTO
rubrics_metrics.description: It is professional misconduct if a practitioner makes false statements of fact or law to the USPTO or fails to correct a false statement of material fact or law previously made to the USPTO by the practitioner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners must ensure accuracy and correct prior misstatements to the USPTO; material false statements are sanctionable.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.503(a) — Managerial responsibility to assure firm measures
rubrics_metrics.description: It is professional misconduct if a practitioner who is a partner, or who possesses comparable managerial authority, fails to make reasonable efforts to ensure that the firm has measures giving reasonable assurance that the person's conduct is compatible with the professional obligations of the practitioner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Firm-level policies, training, and oversight are required to ensure compliance with USPTO professional obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.503(b) — Supervisory duty over non-practitioner assistants
rubrics_metrics.description: It is professional misconduct if a practitioner having direct supervisory authority over a non-practitioner assistant fails to make reasonable efforts to ensure that the non-practitioner's conduct is compatible with the professional obligations of the practitioner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supervising practitioners must supervise employees and contractors (non-practitioners) and ensure their conduct (e.g., client communications, filings) complies with professional rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.503(c)(1) — Ordering or ratifying misconduct by non-practitioners
rubrics_metrics.description: It is professional misconduct if a practitioner orders or ratifies, with knowledge of the conduct, the conduct of non-practitioner assistants which would have violated the USPTO Rules of Professional Conduct if engaged in by the practitioner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Active approval or direction of improper conduct by non-practitioner staff (e.g., unauthorized practice, falsified signatures) is sanctionable.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.503(c)(2) — Duty to take reasonable remedial action
rubrics_metrics.description: It is professional misconduct if a practitioner fails to take reasonable remedial action when the conduct of non-practitioner assistants under the practitioner's supervision violates the Rules and the practitioner knows of the conduct at a time when its consequences can be avoided or mitigated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When supervisors become aware of rule-violating conduct by staff, they must act promptly to mitigate harm (e.g., correct filings, notify affected clients/agency).

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.505 — Assisting in unauthorized practice of law
rubrics_metrics.description: It is professional misconduct if a practitioner assists in the unauthorized practice of law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners must not enable non-lawyers to provide legal advice or represent clients in a manner that constitutes the unauthorized practice of law.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.804(c) — Prohibition on dishonesty, fraud, deceit, misrepresentation
rubrics_metrics.description: It is professional misconduct if a practitioner engages in conduct involving dishonesty, fraud, deceit or misrepresentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deceptive practices in client interactions, filings, or business operations are grounds for discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.804(d) — Prohibition on conduct prejudicial to administration of justice
rubrics_metrics.description: It is professional misconduct if a practitioner engages in conduct prejudicial to the administration of justice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actions undermining the integrity of the trademark system (e.g., impermissible filings) can prejudice the administration of justice and are sanctionable.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.804(i) — Other conduct reflecting adversely on fitness to practice
rubrics_metrics.description: It is professional misconduct if a practitioner engages in other conduct that adversely reflects on the practitioner's fitness to practice before the USPTO.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Broad catchall for conduct that demonstrates unfitness to practice before the Office.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 2.193 & TMEP § 611.01(c) — USPTO trademark electronic signature requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: USPTO trademark signature regulations require all electronic signatures to be personally entered by the named signatory and require that a proper person must sign the trademark document. A person signing electronically must personally enter any combination of letters, numbers, spaces and/or punctuation adopted as a signature placed between two forward slash ('/') symbols in the signature block on the electronic submission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TMEP guidance: All documents must be personally signed; the person identified as signatory must manually enter the elements of the electronic signature. Another person (paralegal, assistant, secretary) may not sign the name of a qualified practitioner or other authorized signatory. Typing the electronic signature of another person is not a valid signature. Impermissibly signed filings (e.g., TEAS Plus, Statements of Use, Combined Declarations) can undermine the integrity of the federal trademark registration process and may lead to invalid registrations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affidavit of Resignation under 37 C.F.R. § 11.27 — Exclusion on consent
rubrics_metrics.description: The Director may approve an Affidavit of Resignation pursuant to 37 C.F.R. § 11.27 and exclude a respondent on consent from practice before the Office in trademark and other non-patent matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An approved affidavit results in exclusion on consent effective as ordered; the OED Director will publish the Final Order and a notice in the Official Gazette consistent with the decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reinstatement consequences under 37 C.F.R. § 11.60 — Presumptions after resignation
rubrics_metrics.description: If and when a person who resigned under an affidavit seeks reinstatement under 37 C.F.R. § 11.60 to practice before the USPTO in trademark/non-patent matters, the OED Director will conclusively presume, for the purpose of determining the application, that the allegations in the related disciplinary complaints are true and that the respondent could not have successfully defended against them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resignation while disciplinary complaints are pending carries the consequence that, for reinstatement purposes, the OED will treat the underlying allegations as conclusively established.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practitioners' obligation not to file or allow filings not signed by the named signatory
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners who represent trademark applicants are reasonably expected not to file, or allow to be filed, declarations that are not signed by the named signatory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because trademark filings bearing declarations are relied upon by the USPTO when examining, registering, and renewing marks, filings not properly signed can adversely affect the registration process and may render resulting registrations invalid if signed by an unauthorized signatory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expectation of knowledge and reasonable supervision of business practices affecting filings
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners are expected to supervise non-practitioner employees and company procedures (e.g., filing manuals, signature protocols, fee-handling) so that business practices do not result in unauthorized signatures, unauthorized practice of law, improper trust handling, or misleading filings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of problematic practices cited include cut-and-paste signatures placed by non-practitioners, non-practitioners giving legal advice on class/specimen/description, retaining USPTO discounted filing fees as company fees without proper escrow/trust handling, and failing to maintain escrow accounts for customer fees or USPTO filing fees. Supervisory practitioners must prevent and remediate such conduct.
